passage:
My name is Alka, and I ran a weekend legal-aid desk in our college. Let me tell you about Francis. One evening a mix-up over a lost bicycle got him taken to the police station for questioning. His friend hissed at him to shout and argue. Instead Francis remembered the desk's leaflet: you have to be given the reason for being held, you may call your family, you may ask for a lawyer.
He took a breath and said, "Sir, may I know the reason? And may I call my family?" The officer gave the reason, and handed over the phone. His family called us, a volunteer lawyer came, and the mix-up was cleared up before midnight. Francis told me later, "I was shaking, but I only asked."

qa.q: What did the leaflet at the desk tell Francis he could do?
qa.a: It said he had to be given the reason for being held, may call his family and may ask for a lawyer.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling as he stood at the station?
qa.a: Francis was frightened and shaky, though he stayed calm enough to ask his questions.

qa.q: What choice inside the story kept the situation from getting worse?
qa.a: Francis did not shout as his friend urged; he took a breath and calmly asked for the reason and to call his family.

qa.q: Why might Francis's friend have hissed at him to shout?
qa.a: The friend was probably scared and wanted to protest, but the calm request ended up working better than arguing.

grounding: A young adult knows basic rights when held by the police, such as asking the reason, calling family and asking for a lawyer, and uses them calmly.

passage:
Rain hammered the roof of the community hall so loudly that Sangeeta, the volunteer lawyer, had to shout over a microphone that kept cutting out. Water dripped near the front row. Noor, twenty, sat with wet sleeves and a soaked notebook, so she wrote on the back of her hand: "reason. call family. lawyer."
"Say it calmly," Sangeeta called. "You are not arguing. You are asking."
Someone at the back shouted, "What if they refuse?"
"Stay polite. Note the officer's name and the time. Reach your family or legal aid."
On the bus home, Noor typed the three points into her phone and sent them to her hostel group. Then she scrubbed the ink off her hand and did not forget a word.

qa.q: What did Noor write on the back of her hand?
qa.a: Noor wrote 'reason. call family. lawyer.'

qa.q: What was Noor feeling as she sat with wet sleeves listening to Sangeeta?
qa.a: Noor was focused and eager to learn, since she wrote the three points on her hand even though her notebook was soaked.

qa.q: What did Noor do after the workshop that spread the learning?
qa.a: She typed the three points into her phone and sent them to her hostel group on the bus home.

qa.q: How does Sangeeta want people to behave if an officer refuses?
qa.a: Sangeeta wants them to stay polite, note the officer's name and the time, and reach family or legal aid, because asking calmly is protective.

grounding: A young adult learns the basics of rights when arrested and knows them calmly without arguing, which is protective.

passage:
Pankaj, twenty, was at the tea stall when a scuffle broke out between two groups near the bus stand. His friend Sachin had only been standing close by, but when the police arrived, they took him along with the others.
Pankaj's heart raced. He wanted to shout that Sachin was innocent. Instead, he remembered the legal-awareness session at college.
He walked up to the officer and said quietly, "Sir, may I know why my friend is being taken? And which police station? I'd like to inform his family."
The officer, surprised by his calm, told him the station and the reason: they were questioning everyone present.
Pankaj called Sachin's father immediately and, on the way, called the legal aid helpline number he'd saved from the session. A volunteer lawyer met them at the station.
Sachin was released that evening after giving a statement. "You didn't argue," he said to Pankaj. "That helped."

qa.q: What did Pankaj ask the officer?
qa.a: He asked, "Sir, may I know why my friend is being taken? And which police station? I'd like to inform his family."

qa.q: What was Pankaj feeling when he wanted to shout?
qa.a: Pankaj felt panicked and protective of Sachin, but he chose calm instead.

qa.q: What made Pankaj's response protective?
qa.a: He calmly asked for the reason and the station, informed Sachin's family, and got a legal aid lawyer involved, without arguing.

qa.q: How might Sachin feel about Pankaj afterwards?
qa.a: Sachin seems grateful and relieved, noticing that Pankaj's calm helped.

grounding: A young adult calmly asks why a friend is taken, informs the family and contacts legal aid, showing that knowing basic rights without arguing is protective.

passage:
"Excuse me, Yamini Ma'am, can I ask something?"
"Of course, Jyoti. That's what this workshop is for."
"If the police take someone for questioning, do they have to say why?"
"Yes. A person who is arrested has to be told the reason. They can inform a family member or friend, and they have the right to speak to a lawyer."
"Even if the police are angry?"
"Especially then. Stay calm. Don't argue or resist. Just ask, politely, 'What is the reason?' and 'May I call my family?' And ask for a lawyer."
"What if they say no?"
"Remember names and times. Your family can contact a legal aid centre or a senior officer."
Jyoti wrote it all down. "My brother was taken last year and we didn't know any of this. We were just scared."
Yamini Ma'am nodded gently. "Now you know. Knowledge helps you stay calm."

qa.q: Who is running the workshop?
qa.a: Yamini Ma'am is running the workshop.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling when she mentioned her brother?
qa.a: Jyoti felt a leftover fear and helplessness from last year, when her family didn't know their rights.

qa.q: What does Yamini Ma'am advise, and why is it protective?
qa.a: She advises staying calm, asking the reason politely, asking to call family and for a lawyer, and noting names and times, which protects without escalating.

qa.q: How might Jyoti's family have felt last year?
qa.a: They were scared and confused, not knowing what they could ask or who to contact.

grounding: At a workshop, a young adult learns the basics of an arrested person's rights and how to use them calmly without arguing.

passage:
When my friend Anirban was taken to the police station after a bike accident last year, I was the only one with him. I'm Rehana, and I was twenty.
My first instinct was to scream at the officers. He wasn't even driving; the other biker had crashed into him. But I remembered a college session on rights.
I asked, calmly, "Sir, is he being arrested, and on what grounds?" The officer said they were recording statements. I asked, "May he call his family?" They let him.
I also called the legal aid number from my phone. A lawyer called the station and spoke to the officer on duty.
By night, Anirban had given his statement and gone home with his father.
Looking back, what saved us wasn't shouting. It was knowing what to ask, and asking politely. I still keep that number saved.

qa.q: What happened to Anirban last year?
qa.a: He was taken to the police station after a bike accident.

qa.q: What did Rehana feel like doing at first?
qa.a: Rehana felt angry and frightened, wanting to scream at the officers because Anirban wasn't driving.

qa.q: What did Rehana do that was protective?
qa.a: Rehana calmly asked about the grounds, asked if Anirban could call family, and contacted legal aid, rather than arguing.

qa.q: How might Anirban have felt with Rehana there?
qa.a: Anirban probably felt less alone and grateful that his friend stayed calm and knew what to ask.

grounding: A young adult calmly uses basic rights knowledge when a friend is taken to a police station, showing that knowing them without arguing is protective.

passage:
Legal aid clinic note, Saturday. Elizabeth Mathew, coordinator.
Kunal, a second-year engineering student who attended our rights workshop last month, came in today to tell us what happened on Tuesday. His roommate was picked up by police after a scuffle outside a tea stall. Kunal said his first urge was to shout at the officers. Instead he stood back, spoke politely, and asked, "Sir, may I know the reason he is being taken?" He was told. He then asked which station, and phoned his roommate's parents and our clinic helpline. Our volunteer lawyer reached the station within two hours. Kunal said his voice shook the whole time, but he kept it low.
What I did next: I asked if he would share this at next month's workshop, and he agreed. I also gave him our wallet card with these basic rights and the helpline number, for his roommate.

qa.q: What did Kunal ask the officers first?
qa.a: He asked, "Sir, may I know the reason he is being taken?"

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling while he spoke to the officers?
qa.a: Kunal was scared and angry, with an urge to shout and a shaking voice, but he kept calm and spoke low.

qa.q: Why did Kunal's calm approach protect his roommate?
qa.a: By politely asking the reason and the station without arguing, and quickly calling the parents and the helpline, he got a lawyer there within two hours.

qa.q: How might the roommate's parents have felt getting Kunal's call?
qa.a: They were probably frightened but also relieved that someone calm told them quickly where their son was and that help was coming.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who knows basic rights on arrest, asks for the reason, contacts family and gets legal help calmly, without arguing.
